title: What not to put on the site for a logistics company
excerpt: Cut the stock container and the globe. Keep one real move and a way to request a quote. A shorter site that states the mode, the limit, and the clock will beat a long performance of taste.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper, marking the path a logistics site should keep and the costume it should lose.
caption: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove from a logistics homepage?
faqs.answer: Remove the stock container, the globe, and any headline that could belong to any carrier. Replace them with one move you can defend, or with a plain sentence about mode and region, plus a way to request a quote. The costume reassures a committee and answers nothing for an operator.

faqs.question: Should a carrier launch with industry pages and a blog?
faqs.answer: Launch the pages that do a job: the offer, the rates and accessorials, the modes you actually run, who answers, one true load, and the quote path. Add a page when the same question arrives twice. Repeated industry pages and an empty journal compete with quote, track, and claims.

faqs.question: How short can the site be?
faqs.answer: Short enough that someone on a phone can find the mode, a refusal or a rate shape, and the quote path without a brand film. The about page should still name who answers, and the services page should still name a limit. Cutting the container is not a reason to become vague.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The logistics company website mistakes that lose an operator are usually there to comfort the team. Cut a stock photo of a shipping container. Keep the work, not a globe, and a clear way to request a quote. A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long one that performs taste.

You can feel the long version in a conference room. It looks complete. It has a map, a manifesto, a logo row, and a sentence about end-to-end solutions. The operator feels something else. They still do not know if you can make the appointment.

## Cut the container and the globe

The container on the water is the signature mistake. It tells a committee that the site looks like logistics. It tells a coordinator nothing about equipment, cutoff, or territory. The same is true of a globe, a glowing network, and a drone shot of a port you do not run.

Replace the frame with a move you can defend, or with type if you cannot show the freight. "Dry van, dock to dock, POD the same day" is a homepage. A rented ship is a delay. If someone puts the container back because the page feels empty, read the sentence out loud. Empty of costume is not empty of offer.

Cut the pictures that smuggle a second decision into the art: two buttons, a fake app, a billboard. The quote path is the decision. The picture should show the work or leave.

While you are in the hero, cut the headline that could sit on any carrier. "Moving what matters" and "Your supply chain partner" are the globe in words. Say the mode, the region, and the action. The team may find it plain. Plain is what the operator can use between two calls.

## Cut the manifesto that comes before the freight

An essay about resilience, passion, or the future of global trade reassures the people who wrote it. It sits in front of the only question on the table: can you move this. Move any mission language below the move, the boundary, and the quote. If a sentence does not help someone request a rate or walk away, it does not belong in the first two screens.

Google's people-first content guidance is a useful filter. A page should help a visitor do the task they came for, and it should be specific enough that it cannot be pasted onto a random competitor. A paragraph about disruption can be pasted anywhere. A cutoff and a refusal cannot.

Cut fake urgency. "Limited capacity this week" with no rule. Countdown banners. "We're hiring" as the first thing a shipper sees, unless the page is the jobs page. Manufactured pressure is a taste performance. Coordinators have a good ear for it, because their own customers try it on them.

Cut the software tour if the product is the truck. A portal can be a sentence: status at pickup and delivery, or a login for people who already have an account. A homepage that leads with a dashboard screenshot has confused a carrier for a software company. The operator did not come to buy a login.

## Cut proof you cannot stand behind

Logo grids of ports, software vendors, and associations that are not a safety fact. "99% on time" with no denominator. Quotes you wrote and attributed to a shipper. Awards that need a footnote. A coverage map with a pin in every state you once emailed.

Keep one load you can explain: constraint, decision, outcome. Keep a number you can find in a file. Keep a certification only if you can say what it changes for the freight. Everything else is costume, and costume is what this buyer is trying to see past.

If you are early, a short true account beats a theatrical network. "We run dry van in four states, and the owner still confirms appointments" is a site. Publishing the theatrical version because the true one feels small is how you end up defending copy while a load sits.

Also cut partner marks that imply you perform a service you subcontract and never see. If a drayage firm is not you, do not let their world leak into your hero. Say what you do. Let the other work be a sentence with a boundary, or leave it off until you can answer the phone about it.

## Cut pages that only look like a company

A blog with no point of view. A press page with no press. An industries section that repeats one paragraph six times. A careers page when you are not hiring. A "technology" page that is a list of nouns. These pages create menu items that compete with quote, rates, track, and claims.

Ship the pages that answer a job. Homepage, rates and accessorials, the modes you run, who answers, one true load, the quote path, and a plain privacy note. Add a page when a real question arrives twice. Do not add a page because a template had a slot called Insights.

Title each page for the job. Google's guidance on title links favors titles that describe the page and that are not a repeated slogan. "Acme | The future of freight | Rates" wastes the label in a tab and in a search result. "Rates and accessorials" does the job. The brand can live in its usual place without eating the front of every title.

Delete the stock illustrations of globes, handshakes, and containers. They are the visual form of the manifesto. Empty space is a better neighbor for a true sentence than a picture that argues with it.

## Keep the move and the door

After the cuts, the first screen still does three things. It shows one move a dispatcher would recognize. It states a refusal or points at the rate shape. It offers one way to request a quote, with the facts to have ready and the window you will keep.

The about page still names who answers. The services page still states a boundary. The navigation still uses their words. Cutting is not an excuse to become vague. It is how those few statements become visible on a phone in a yard.

Read the shorter site out loud in the time a person will actually give it. If you can say the mode, the limit, and the next step without a brand film, you have the site. If you miss one, put it back in words. Do not put the container back.

A practical rule for the room: a new section has to earn its place by removing one. If additions are free, the manifesto returns within a month, usually as a campaign. The archive can hold the longer story for anyone who asks. The homepage cannot.

## How the long site gets argued back

Someone will say the page feels empty. Often they mean it does not look like a national brand. The operator is not grading you on whether you look national. They are grading you on whether the freight moves under a rule they can predict.

Someone will want both a quote button and a track button and a careers button in the hero, for fairness. Tracking matters to people who already shipped. It does not need the first screen on the day you are trying to win the load. Put it in the header, plainly, and leave the emphasis on the quote.

Someone will want to keep a section because the photograph was expensive. Sunk cost is not a reason to tax every future coordinator. Thank the frame. If it shows your equipment, crop it to the equipment and write a caption. If it shows a ship, let it go.

## A pass you can run on the live site

Open the homepage on a phone and circle anything that is not the move, a limit, or the quote. For each circle, write the reader it serves. If the only reader is the team, a template, or a slide from last year's offsite, remove it and look again the next day before you restore it.

Do the same with the menu. Any item you cannot connect to a job from the last ten real calls is a candidate. Park it. A shorter menu is reversible. A long menu you are embarrassed to read aloud is not a brand asset.

Then read the remaining lines for claims you could not defend with a file. Superlatives, unnamed quotes, coverage you do not run, and round percentages without a denominator. Replace each with the specific fact or delete the line. The page will sound quieter. Quieter is what a skeptical coordinator hears as a desk that knows its own limits.

Do not wait for a redesign to do this. The cuts can ship as copy and pictures on the current site. A new visual system that keeps the container and the manifesto has not started the work.

The same costume shows up when the buyer needs specs and a way to talk about an object, rather than a move. That page is [what the homepage has to prove for a manufacturer](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-manufacturer).

To see how a public site can lead with the work and leave the costume out, look through [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
